note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain what a presentation tests and read its brief

evidence.title: Presentation brief mapped to learning outcomes
evidence.example: You take a presentation brief and its marking criteria and link each criterion to the learning outcome it tests, using Biggs' (1996) idea of constructive alignment. You then write a short list, in your own words, of what the presentation is really asking you to show. This shows you can read a brief for what it tests, not just its topic (for example, a sport science brief on warm-up routines that rewards applying evidence, not only describing it).
evidence.artefact: An annotated copy of the brief with each criterion linked to a learning outcome, and a five-point list of what it tests.

evidence.title: Purpose notes for a team huddle talk at work
evidence.example: Your supervisor at a supermarket asks you to give a five-minute talk at the morning team huddle on a new returns process. Before preparing, you write down what the talk needs to achieve, who will be listening, how long you have and how you will know it worked, and you check this with your supervisor. This shows you can read a brief before building anything (for example, the real test being that staff can process a return without calling a manager).
evidence.artefact: Your written notes on purpose, audience and time, with your supervisor's confirmation or correction.

genericOutcomes.title: Brief read for its hidden test
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a presentation brief defines its intended audience, required form and the ideas it is meant to make clear.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a presentation task and its assessment criteria, you work out, before planning any content, what the task is actually testing: the ideas it wants explained, the audience it is aimed at and the form the explanation must take. You write this out as a short statement of intent and check it against the stated criteria rather than against habit. This demonstrates that communicating a subject clearly depends on matching form and content to audience before any talk is built.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written statement of what the brief tests, its intended audience and the required form of explanation.

genericOutcomes.title: Audience and format checked before drafting
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify the audience and form required by a presentation brief and use that to guide what is planned before any content is drafted.
genericOutcomes.example: Before you start building a talk, you identify who will be listening, what they already know and what form of explanation will suit them best, whether that is a short briefing, a visual walkthrough or a question and answer session. You then draft your content to match that audience and form, rather than reusing material written for a different purpose. This shows you can communicate a subject clearly to different audiences and in different forms, which is the real test any presentation sets.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short audience and format analysis used to shape a talk's content before it is drafted.
grounding: professional: Matches the content, length and format of an explanation to who is listening before drafting it.

capabilities.statement: Build a presentation to a brief through the five steps

evidence.title: Storyboard built through the five steps and compared with Monroe
evidence.example: You build a short presentation to a set brief, working through the five steps your module teaches, with a hook, a main body and a conclusion. You compare your structure with Monroe's Motivated Sequence (Monroe 1935): attention, need, satisfaction, visualisation and action, and note which stages your opening and close cover. This shows a structured build, not slides assembled at the last minute (for example, an environmental engineering talk that opens with a flood photo before setting out drainage options).
evidence.artefact: A storyboard or slide outline labelled with the five steps, the hook, main body and conclusion, and the matching Monroe stage.

evidence.title: Open day talk planned as a student ambassador
evidence.example: As a student ambassador, you are asked to give a ten-minute talk to visiting sixth formers about life on your course. You plan it to the brief, with its purpose, audience and time, then build a hook, three main points and a clear close. This shows you can build a presentation to someone else's brief (for example, opening with a question about the most surprising thing you learned in first-year chemistry).
evidence.artefact: Your plan and slides for the open day talk, with brief written feedback from the outreach officer who organised it.
grounding: professional: Prepares a talk or briefing to a set purpose, audience and time.
professional: Vitae RDF D2: communication and dissemination

genericOutcomes.title: Five step structure justified against a sequence model
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can describe a five step structure for building a presentation and explain how it guides an audience from attention to action.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a presentation brief and build its structure through five set steps, producing a hook, a main body and a conclusion rather than a loose list of points. You then test that structure against a recognised sequence for moving an audience from attention to action, checking that your opening earns attention and your closing asks for something specific. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by giving it a shape an audience can follow, not simply a shape you find comfortable to write.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A labelled storyboard showing the five steps and the stage of the sequence model each section covers.

genericOutcomes.title: Hook, body and close built to a brief
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can build a presentation to a given brief using five set steps, producing an opening, a main body and a conclusion for a specific audience.
genericOutcomes.example: You are given a brief for a talk, including its purpose, audience and time limit, and you build it through a hook that earns attention, a main body of a few clear points and a conclusion that asks for something specific. You check the finished structure against the original brief before delivering it. This shows you can communicate a subject clearly in a form built for a particular audience, rather than reusing a structure that suited a different occasion entirely.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A finished talk plan showing the hook, main points and conclusion, checked against the original brief.
grounding: professional: Prepares a talk or briefing to a set purpose, audience and time.

capabilities.statement: Practise to time and fix what does not work

evidence.title: Timed rehearsal log structured by Kolb's learning cycle
evidence.example: You rehearse a presentation at least three times, timing and recording each run. After each one you work through Kolb's (1984) experiential learning cycle: the run itself, watching the recording, working out why a section did not work, and trying a change in the next run. This shows you check your own performance and fix it (for example, a history student trimming a long background section on the causes of the First World War to finish inside ten minutes).
evidence.artefact: A rehearsal log of three timed runs, noting what you changed after each and the final timing.

evidence.title: Society welcome speech tested and cut to time
evidence.example: Before speaking at your society's welcome event, you run through your talk with two committee members, timing it and asking what was unclear. You fix the parts that do not work, then run it again until it fits the slot. This shows practice to time and honest correction in a real setting (for example, a drama society welcome speech that first ran at four minutes against a two-minute slot).
evidence.artefact: Your before and after notes or script with timings, plus a short message from a committee member on the changes.

genericOutcomes.title: Timed run reviewed for what did not work
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how timing a rehearsal and identifying what did not work supports improving a presentation before it is delivered.
genericOutcomes.example: You time a run of a talk and, straight after, identify the specific moment where it ran long or lost its thread, rather than making a vague judgement that it went badly. You name what did not work, decide on one change, and plan to test that change in the next run. This demonstrates checking your own performance against a clear measure, time, and using that check to decide what to fix rather than simply repeating the same run again unchanged.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note naming one problem from a timed run, the change planned and the next run's result.
grounding: benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Fix identified and tested in the next run
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can time a rehearsal of a presentation, identify one specific problem it reveals and make a targeted change before the next attempt.
genericOutcomes.example: After timing a run of a talk, you identify one thing that did not work, whether it overran, lost the audience or missed a point, and you make a specific change before the next attempt. You keep doing this until the talk fits its time and holds together, rather than stopping once you feel ready. This shows practising to time and genuinely fixing problems, not just repeating a run and hoping it goes better by chance alone.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short log of timed runs, each with one named problem and the change made before the next attempt.
grounding: professional: Times a rehearsal, acts on honest feedback and cuts content until it fits the slot given.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Design effective, accessible visual aids ("less is more")

evidence.title: Slide redesign justified with cognitive load theory
evidence.example: You redesign a cluttered slide deck using cognitive load theory (Sweller 1988): you cut text that repeats what you say, split dense slides, and keep one idea per slide to reduce unnecessary load. You also check accessibility, including colour contrast, font size, alternative text and captions, and justify each change in a short design note (for example, a nutrition slide turning a paragraph of figures into one labelled chart).
evidence.artefact: Before and after slides with a design rationale and a completed accessibility checklist, such as the output of a built-in checker.

evidence.title: Accessible slide loop for a local museum entrance
evidence.example: Volunteering at a local museum, you design a slide loop for the screen in the entrance hall. You choose large text, strong contrast and images with short captions that visitors can take in within seconds, and you test it with a few visitors and staff. This shows you can design visual aids that work for a real, mixed audience (for example, replacing a dense timeline of the town's mills with three photographs and one line each).
evidence.artefact: The final slide loop, a note of the accessibility checks you ran, and feedback from the volunteer manager.
grounding: professional: Prepares presentations and slide decks for colleagues, clients or the public, accessible to the audience.

genericOutcomes.title: Slide clutter cut using a load reduction principle
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse how reducing visual clutter and applying accessibility standards improves an audience's ability to follow a presentation's visual aids.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a slide deck full of dense text and small images, you apply a principle of cutting unnecessary cognitive load: removing text that only repeats speech, splitting busy slides into two simpler ones, and keeping a single idea per slide. You then check each redesigned slide against basic accessibility standards, including contrast and text size, before judging it finished. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by shaping visual aids around what an audience can actually take in during a talk.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A redesigned slide set with a short note explaining each cut or split and the accessibility checks applied.

genericOutcomes.title: Accessible visuals tested with real viewers
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can redesign a set of visual aids to cut unnecessary content and meet accessibility standards, checking each change against how real viewers respond.
genericOutcomes.example: You design the visual aids for a talk and test them on people who were not involved in making them, checking that text is large enough, contrast is strong enough and images make sense without your spoken explanation. You adjust anything that confused a viewer before the final version goes out. This shows you can communicate a subject clearly in a visual form to an audience that includes people with different needs, not just the audience you originally had in mind.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A tested slide set with a short log of viewer feedback and the changes made in response.
grounding: professional: Prepares presentations and slide decks for colleagues, clients or the public, accessible to the audience.

capabilities.statement: Adapt delivery to different presentation formats

evidence.title: One project delivered as talk and poster, analysed with Bitzer
evidence.example: You take one piece of work and deliver it in two assessment formats: a ten-minute individual talk and a poster session. Using Bitzer's (1968) rhetorical situation, with its exigence, audience and constraints, you analyse what each format demands and justify the delivery choices you made for each (for example, a geography fieldwork project on coastal erosion, told as a story in the talk and as a two-minute walk-through at the poster).
evidence.artefact: A recording of the talk and the poster, with a one-page comparison of the delivery choices made for each format.

evidence.title: Union update delivered in person and as an online video
evidence.example: As a students' union course representative, you present the same update on library opening hours twice: in person to the union council, and as a short recorded video for students online. You change the length, detail and pace for each audience and medium, and explain why. This shows you adapt delivery to the occasion (for example, cutting the budget detail from the video and adding captions for students watching on phones).
evidence.artefact: Your council slides and the online video, with a short note explaining how and why you changed delivery for each.
grounding: professional: Adapts delivery to the occasion: pitch, briefing, conference talk, poster, interview or online meeting.

genericOutcomes.title: Delivery choices tested against a rhetorical model
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse how the demands of a presentation format shape the pacing, level of detail and structure a speaker should choose.
genericOutcomes.example: Given one set of content to present in two different formats, you use a model of the rhetorical situation, its exigence, audience and constraints, to work out what each format actually demands before you build it. You then justify, in writing, why the pacing, detail and structure differ between the two versions rather than letting the differences happen by accident. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by treating form as a deliberate choice rather than an afterthought bolted on late.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written justification comparing the delivery choices made for two different formats of the same content.

genericOutcomes.title: Content rebuilt for a different delivery format
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can adapt the same content for a different presentation format, rebuilding its pacing, detail and structure rather than simply shortening the original.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to deliver the same material in a new format, for example turning a planned talk into a poster or a live briefing into a recorded video. You identify what the new format allows and restricts, then rebuild the pacing, level of detail and structure to suit it, rather than simply shortening the original. This shows you can adapt delivery to the occasion, communicating the same subject clearly whatever form the audience actually needs to receive it in on the day.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Two versions of the same content built for different formats, with a short note on what changed and why.
grounding: professional: Adapts delivery to the occasion: pitch, briefing, conference talk, poster, interview or online meeting.

capabilities.statement: Open engagingly and manage own nerves

evidence.title: Tested hooks and a nerves plan based on Yerkes-Dodson
evidence.example: You draft and test two possible hooks for an assessed presentation and choose one with reasons. You also write a nerves plan based on the Yerkes-Dodson law (Yerkes and Dodson 1908), which links arousal to performance in an inverted U, so you aim to use some nervous energy rather than remove it, with breathing and a well-rehearsed first minute (for example, a psychology student opening with a quick show of hands on last night's sleep).
evidence.artefact: Your two draft hooks with the reason for your choice, a pre-presentation nerves plan and a short reflection afterwards.

evidence.title: Season launch talk to parents as a volunteer coach
evidence.example: As a volunteer coach at a junior rugby club, you speak to parents at the season launch. You open with a short story that gets their attention, then keep composed when a parent challenges the training schedule in front of everyone. This shows you can open engagingly and manage your nerves when the pressure is real (for example, pausing, thanking the parent and offering to talk afterwards rather than rushing an answer).
evidence.artefact: A short video clip or the head coach's written feedback on your opening and composure, with your own reflection.
grounding: professional: Engages an audience from the start and stays composed when presenting under pressure.

genericOutcomes.title: Opening designed to earn attention from the first line
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a deliberately designed opening and a managed level of arousal help a speaker engage an audience from the first moment.
genericOutcomes.example: Before building the rest of a talk, you design its opening line by line, testing more than one option against what will actually earn attention from a specific audience rather than what feels comfortable to say. You use an understanding of arousal and performance to pitch your energy deliberately, neither flat nor overexcited, and you rehearse the opening until it no longer needs notes. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by treating the first moment of a talk as a deliberate design choice, not luck.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A tested opening line with the reasoning for choosing it over an alternative, and a note on rehearsed delivery.

genericOutcomes.title: Composure kept through an unplanned challenge
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can open a presentation engagingly and stay composed when faced with an unplanned challenge from the audience, without losing its structure.
genericOutcomes.example: While presenting, you are interrupted or challenged by someone in the audience in a way you had not planned for. You pause rather than rushing a reply, acknowledge the point fairly, and either answer briefly or agree to return to it later, then pick the talk back up without losing the audience. This shows you can stay composed under real pressure and keep communicating a subject clearly, rather than letting one difficult moment derail the rest of the talk entirely.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account of an unplanned challenge faced while presenting and how composure was kept, with feedback.
grounding: professional: Engages an audience from the start and stays composed when presenting under pressure.

capabilities.statement: Present in professional formats (pitch, conference poster, viva-style interview)

evidence.title: Enterprise pitch and poster built on Toulmin's argument model
evidence.example: You prepare a three-minute pitch for an enterprise competition and build its core case with Toulmin's (1958) model: the claim, the data behind it, the warrant linking them, and a rebuttal that answers the obvious objection. You then carry the same argument into a conference-style poster, judging what each format needs to cut or keep (for example, a pitch for a campus food-waste app backed by a two-week trial in one hall of residence).
evidence.artefact: Your pitch deck and poster, annotated with the Toulmin elements, and the judges' feedback sheet.

evidence.title: Assessment centre presentation and panel interview
evidence.example: You apply for a graduate scheme or placement that uses a presentation-based assessment centre. You prepare the set presentation, deliver it to the panel and answer their follow-up questions in interview style, treating it as a professional performance rather than a class exercise. This shows you can present in a real professional format (for example, a civil engineering applicant presenting a ten-minute case for a bridge maintenance plan and defending its costs).
evidence.artefact: Your assessment centre slides and preparation notes, with written feedback from the employer or a careers adviser's mock panel record.
grounding: professional: Pitches to clients, presents at conferences and performs in selection or assessment interviews.
professional: Vitae RDF D2: communication and dissemination

genericOutcomes.title: Case built with claim, data, warrant and rebuttal
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct an argument for a professional pitch using claim, evidence, warrant and rebuttal so that each step of its reasoning is explicit.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a position to argue in a short pitch, you build its case using a structured argument model: stating the claim plainly, backing it with specific data, making explicit the warrant that links the data to the claim, and preparing a rebuttal for the most obvious objection. You then check the finished case holds together without your slides as a prop. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by making every step of an argument visible rather than merely asserted on a slide.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written case broken into claim, data, warrant and rebuttal, used to brief the final pitch.

genericOutcomes.title: Pitch defended under direct questioning
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can deliver a pitch in a professional format and defend its weakest points under direct questioning, conceding fairly where the evidence is limited.
genericOutcomes.example: You deliver a short pitch in a professional format and are then questioned directly on its weakest points by people who were not involved in preparing it. You hold your position where the evidence supports it, concede the parts that are genuinely weaker, and avoid repeating rehearsed lines when a specific question is asked. This shows you can present in a professional format and defend the substance of an argument, not just perform a fixed script regardless of the question.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A record of the pitch delivered and the questions faced, with a short note on how each was answered.
grounding: professional: Pitches to clients, presents at conferences and performs in selection or assessment interviews.

capabilities.statement: Work in a group, leading and resolving conflict

evidence.title: Team ground rules and a conflict worked through with Tuckman
evidence.example: At the start of a group project you lead the team in agreeing ground rules and roles, drawing on Gibbs' (1994) Learning in Teams. When conflict surfaces, you use Tuckman's (1965) stages of group development to name what is happening and steer the team through it, then record what the rules let you do. This shows leadership and conflict resolution based on a model (for example, a computing team split over whether to rewrite or patch a prototype).
evidence.artefact: The team's agreed ground rules, meeting notes showing the conflict and how it was resolved, and a 400-word reflection on your leadership.

evidence.title: Leading volunteers through a budget dispute at a charity event
evidence.example: As the committee lead for a student society's charity event, you coordinate a team of volunteers over several weeks. When two members disagree sharply about the budget, you meet them together, set out the options and agree a way forward that keeps the event on track. This shows you can lead and mediate in a real team (for example, splitting the budget between venue and publicity after both sides showed their costings).
evidence.artefact: Event planning minutes, a short account of how you mediated, and a note or reference from the society's staff adviser.
grounding: professional: Works in and leads teams, mediating disagreements to keep work on track.
professional: Vitae RDF D1: working with others

genericOutcomes.title: Team stage named and used to resolve conflict
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a response to team conflict by naming the group's stage of development rather than treating the friction as purely personal.
genericOutcomes.example: When a team you are part of hits visible conflict, you use a recognised model of group development to name the stage the team is in, rather than treating the friction as simply personal, and you choose a response suited to that stage: clarifying roles, surfacing disagreement openly, or re-agreeing ground rules. You then record what changed afterwards. This demonstrates working effectively with others by diagnosing a team problem before trying to fix it blindly.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account naming the group's stage of development, the response chosen and the outcome recorded.

genericOutcomes.title: Disagreement mediated to keep a team on track
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can mediate a disagreement between team members, steering the group toward a decision both can accept while keeping the work moving.
genericOutcomes.example: Two members of a team you are working in disagree sharply about how to proceed, and the disagreement threatens to stall progress. You bring both people together, let each set out their reasoning, and steer the group toward a decision that both can accept and that keeps the work moving. You follow up afterwards to check the agreement held. This shows you can lead and mediate within a real team, not simply avoid the conflict until it passes on its own.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the disagreement, how it was mediated, the agreed way forward and a later check in.
grounding: professional: Works in and leads teams, mediating disagreements to keep work on track.

capabilities.statement: Present and defend an argument with an academic voice under questioning

evidence.title: Recorded question session analysed for stance
evidence.example: You present your dissertation argument and take questions, then review the recording using Hyland's (2005) model of stance: where you hedged, where you committed, and where you claimed the position as your own. You note answers where you gave ground too quickly or overclaimed, and redraft them with authority. This shows you can defend an argument in an academic voice (for example, a social policy student defending qualitative interviews to a sceptical examiner).
evidence.artefact: The recorded presentation and questions, with three answers transcribed, annotated for stance and redrafted.
grounding: model: Stance and engagement model of academic interaction (Hyland 2005)

evidence.title: Research presentation defended at a student conference
evidence.example: You present your own research at a student or early-career conference and take questions from an audience that includes specialists. You hold your position where the evidence supports it, concede limits openly, and keep a clear academic voice when challenged. This shows you can argue a position and answer challenge in a professional forum (for example, a marine biology student defending a sampling method that a researcher in the audience questions).
evidence.artefact: The conference abstract and slides, a record of the questions and your answers, and feedback from the session chair or a mentor.
grounding: professional: Argues a position and answers challenges from colleagues, clients or panels.
professional: Vitae RDF D2: communication and dissemination

genericOutcomes.title: Stance checked across a set of recorded answers
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique the stance taken in a recorded argument, judging where language overclaimed or hedged relative to the strength of the evidence.
genericOutcomes.example: After presenting an argument and fielding questions, you review your recorded answers against a model of stance: identifying where your language hedged more than the evidence required and where it overclaimed beyond what you could support. You rewrite the weakest answers so the confidence of the language matches the strength of the evidence behind it. This demonstrates communicating a subject clearly by controlling how authoritative you sound relative to what you can actually defend under questioning.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short set of redrafted answers with the original and revised stance marked for each.
grounding: model: Stance and engagement model of academic interaction (Hyland 2005)

genericOutcomes.title: Challenge answered without losing the argument
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can answer a direct challenge to the weakest part of an argument, acknowledging its limit while justifying why the overall position still holds.
genericOutcomes.example: During questions after a presentation, someone directly challenges the weakest part of your argument. You answer by acknowledging the specific limit they have identified, then explaining why your overall position still holds given the evidence available, rather than either collapsing the argument or dismissing the challenge. This shows you can argue a position and answer a direct challenge from colleagues, clients or a panel while keeping both your credibility and the substance of the argument intact.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short transcript or note of a direct challenge faced and the answer given, with the reasoning behind it.
grounding: professional: Argues a position and answers challenges from colleagues, clients or panels.
